title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: every rule of second year at once

questions.prompt: Put the bracketed word in the correct form: "The company answered every ___ within two working days. (COMPLAIN)"

options.text: complain
complained
complaining
complaint

questions.explanation: Every is followed by a singular countable noun, and the noun English builds on complain is "complaint": it changes the end of the verb instead of adding a full syllable, as growth does on grow. "complain" is the verb itself and cannot follow every. "complaining" is the -ing form, which would need no determiner in front of it. "complained" is a past form, and a past verb can never fill a noun slot.

questions.prompt: One part has been deleted from this passage. "(1) On the first Saturday of the holidays we drove down to the coast ___. (2) My grandmother sang the whole way, and my two cousins counted the lorries. (3) The sea was flat and grey when we arrived, and the beach was empty." Which part fits the gap?

options.text: with my grandmother and my two cousins
and the beach there was completely empty
especially the fresh fish restaurants
however the motorway was very busy that day

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 speaks of My grandmother and my two cousins as if you already knew they were in the car, and nothing before the gap has put them there, so the missing part is "with my grandmother and my two cousins". "and the beach there was completely empty" repeats what sentence 3 says a few words later, and a text never states the same fact twice in three lines. "however the motorway was very busy that day" opens a contrast with something that has not been said yet, and the passage never mentions the traffic. "especially the fresh fish restaurants" points at restaurants the passage never mentions, so it has nothing to attach to. The method is always the same: find the word that has lost what it points back at.

questions.prompt: Read: "The head teacher gave the winners their certificates last Friday." The school magazine wants to report the fact without naming the head teacher. Which sentence does that correctly?

options.text: The winners gave their certificates last Friday.
The winners was given their certificates last Friday.
The winners were given their certificates last Friday.
Their certificates were given the winners last Friday.

questions.explanation: Dropping the doer is exactly what the passive is for, and a verb with two objects passivises most naturally from the person: "The winners were given their certificates last Friday." "The winners was given their certificates last Friday." hands a plural subject a singular be. "Their certificates were given the winners last Friday." starts from the other object, which is possible, but it then drops the to that the person needs: given to the winners. "The winners gave their certificates last Friday." is not a passive at all; it is an active sentence that makes the winners the people handing the certificates out.

questions.prompt: Report this sentence: The engineer said: "I will finish the plans before the holiday."

options.text: The engineer said that he will finish the plans before the holiday.
The engineer said that he would finish the plans before the holiday.
The engineer said that he would have finished the plans before the holiday.
The engineer said that I would finish the plans before the holiday.

questions.explanation: After a reporting verb in the past, will steps back to would and the speaker's I becomes he: "The engineer said that he would finish the plans before the holiday." "The engineer said that he will finish the plans before the holiday." moves the pronoun but leaves will untouched, so only half the report is done. "The engineer said that I would finish the plans before the holiday." does the opposite and keeps the engineer's own I, which now points at the person reporting. "The engineer said that he would have finished the plans before the holiday." backshifts twice and turns a promise into a finished job.

questions.prompt: Complete: "In a modern hospital the computer is ___ the scanner: neither of the two can work without the other."

options.text: as important as
as important than
more important as
so important as

questions.explanation: The second half of the sentence puts the two machines on exactly the same level, and English levels two things with as + adjective + as: "as important as". "more important as" is wrong twice over: it mixes the comparative more with as, and a comparative would place one machine above the other, which the second half denies. "as important than" replaces the second as with than, a word kept for comparatives. "so important as" is only used in negative sentences, as in not so important as the scanner.

questions.prompt: "The company was forced to close its second factory." Which sentence says exactly the same thing?

options.text: The company let something close its second factory.
The company made something close its second factory.
The company was made close its second factory.
Something made the company close its second factory.

questions.explanation: Was forced to is a passive: the company did not choose, something outside obliged it. In the active, obliging is make + object + base verb, which gives "Something made the company close its second factory." "The company made something close its second factory." turns the sentence round and makes the company the one doing the obliging. "The company let something close its second factory." replaces obligation with permission, the opposite idea. "The company was made close its second factory." keeps the passive but forgets that make gets its to back there: was made to close is the correct form.
